title: Responders, non-responders and dose
goal: Judge whether someone is a true non-responder, explain how Montero and Lundby made non-response disappear with more training and what limits that result, and decide what an athlete should do after a flat training block.

steps.title: Real differences, shaky labels
steps.text:
From *Noise, worthwhile changes and non-responders* you know the trap: one test before and one after can't separate a small gain from noise. So are the differences between people real at all?

One study tackled it head on. Of 36 untrained middle-aged adults, a training group walked or jogged three times a week for a year, with extra VO₂max tests at 3, 6 and 9 months; the others were a control group for 6 months. With that many tests, true differences in response big enough to matter could be shown [[c:h18-real]].

But when the 20 people in the training group were sorted into responders and [non-responders](g:non-responder) by different accepted methods, only 11 got the same label every time [[c:h18-labels]]. People truly differ; naming who is who is much harder.

claims.text: With repeated testing during a year of training, relevant individual differences in VO₂max response could be shown.

evidence.quote: Individual training response of relevant magnitude (>0.2 × baseline variability in V̇o2max) could be demonstrated by several approaches.

claims.text: Only 11 of 20 participants in the training group were classified the same way across methods, which limits responder labels.

evidence.quote: Regarding the classification of individuals, only 11 of 20 subjects were consistently classified, demonstrating remarkable disagreement between approaches.
These results are in support of relevant interindividual variability in training efficacy and stress the limitations of a responder classification.

steps.title: Montero and Lundby: more sessions, fewer non-responders
steps.text:
Montero and Lundby asked whether non-response depends on the dose. 78 healthy adults trained for 6 weeks in five groups: one, two, three, four or five 60-minute sessions a week. Fitness was measured as peak power in a ramp test ([maximal aerobic power](g:maximal-aerobic-power)), and a non-responder was anyone whose change stayed within the test's [typical error](g:typical-error), ±3.96% [[c:ml-design]]. Typical error depends on the lab, the test and the people measured, so it can be far bigger than the ~0.9% ramp-test figure in the testing module.

The share of non-responders fell with each extra session:

| sessions a week | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| non-responders | 69% | 40% | 29% | 0% | 0% |

That is a [dose–response](g:dose-response): the more training, the fewer people left behind [[c:ml-dose]].

claims.text: 78 healthy adults trained 1–5 × 60 min a week for 6 weeks; non-response meant a change in maximal power within the typical error (±3.96%).

evidence.quote: Seventy-eight healthy adults were divided into five groups (1-5) respectively comprising one, two, three, four and five 60 min exercise sessions per week but otherwise following an identical 6-week endurance training (ET) programme.
Non-response was defined as any change in CRF, determined by maximal incremental exercise power output (Wmax ), within the typical error of measurement (±3.96%).

claims.text: Non-responders made up 69%, 40%, 29%, 0% and 0% of the groups training 1–5 times a week.

evidence.quote: In groups 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5, 69%, 40%, 29%, 0% and 0% of individuals, respectively, were non-responders.

steps.title: Responder or not?
steps.problem: In a study that calls any change within ±3.96% a non-response, a cyclist's ramp-test peak power goes from 280 to 288 W. How is she classed?
steps: 2.9% is inside ±3.96%, so she is classed a non-responder, even though her power rose. The label says the gain is too small to tell apart from noise, not that she didn't improve.

steps.title: Non-response abolished
steps.text:
Then came the key step. Everyone classed as a non-responder did a second 6-week block with two extra sessions a week. After it, non-response was gone in every single person [[c:ml-abolish]].

What made the difference? Gains in power followed gains in VO₂max, and the best predictor of the VO₂max gain was the rise in [haemoglobin mass](g:haemoglobin-mass), the blood's total oxygen carrier [[c:ml-hb]].

A different stimulus can work too. In a [crossover study](g:crossover-study), 21 active adults did 3 weeks of steady training and 3 weeks of sprint intervals. Who gained from one didn't predict who gained from the other [[c:bo-switch]].

claims.text: After a second 6-week block with two extra sessions a week, non-response was eliminated in all individuals.

evidence.quote: After the second ET period, non-response was eliminated in all individuals.

claims.text: The change in VO₂max determined the power response, and total haemoglobin mass was the strongest determinant of VO₂max.

evidence.quote: The change in V̇O2 max with exercise training independently determined Wmax response
In turn, total haemoglobin mass was the strongest independent determinant of V̇O2 max

claims.text: Individual changes after endurance training and after sprint interval training were not positively related.

evidence.quote: No significant positive relationships were observed between END and SIT for individual changes in any variable.

debate.question: Do true non-responders to endurance training exist?

sides.position: Hardly: most 'non-response' is too small a dose, the wrong stimulus or test noise; raise the dose or change the plan and everyone improves.
People truly differ in how much they gain from the same plan, partly through their genes, so some gain very little from a given dose.

steps.title: How strong is 'non-response abolished'?
steps.text:
Look at the design before you repeat the slogan.

- **No control group:** nobody was tested without training. A critic called this a strong limitation: without one, changes that would have happened anyway (noise, getting used to the test) can't be removed [[c:ml-no-control]].
- **Dose mixed with time:** the second block added sessions *and* 6 more weeks, so the effect of dose can't be split from the effect of time [[c:ml-time]].
- **Small groups:** about 16 people per group (78 ÷ 5).
- **A question to ask:** only those with the smallest first change went on. Would they have scored higher next time anyway, through [regression to the mean](g:regression-to-the-mean)? The design can't tell.

The direction fits other work; 'everyone, without exception' is the weak part.

claims.text: Montero and Lundby had no non-exercising control group, a strong limitation, since designs without one can't separate training effects from changes that would have happened anyway.

evidence.quote: The absence of a non‐exercising comparator arm in the study of Montero and Lundby represents a strong limitation in this

Designs without a control group (or control condition) (ie, designs 1, 2 and 3) cannot isolate changes due to treatment (eg, exercise training) from changes that would have occurred in the absence of treatment.

claims.text: Because the second block added both sessions and weeks, the effect of dose can't be isolated from the effect of time.

evidence.quote: difficult to isolate the contribution of the training dose to the CRF response from the contribution of the time component

steps.title: What it means for you
steps.text:
Expert consensus: people really do respond differently to the same training dose, and genes are part of it [[c:ro-variable]]. But one flat block doesn't make you a non-responder.

If a block doesn't move your numbers:

1. **Check the noise:** retest, or track a measure across the block, before deciding.
2. **Look wider:** in the crossover study, everyone gained in at least one measure (VO₂max, [lactate threshold](g:lactate-threshold) or heart rate at a set workload) [[c:bo-any]].
3. **Change the dose or the stimulus:** more sessions, or intervals instead of steady work.
4. **Skip the gene test:** it can't tell you your trainability.

And expect smaller gains as you get fitter (*How trainable is VO₂max?*).

claims.text: There is strong evidence that the same training dose leads to variable responses, with a genetic component.

evidence.quote: There is strong evidence from both animal and human studies that exercise training doses lead to variable responses. A genetic component contributes to exercise training response variability.

claims.text: Every participant responded in at least one measure after doing both endurance and sprint interval training.

evidence.quote: Interestingly, all individuals responded in at least one variable when exposed to both END and SIT.

points: With repeated testing and a control group, true differences in training response show up; labelling individuals as non-responders is still unreliable.
Montero and Lundby: non-responders fell from 69% with one session a week to 0% with four or five; a dose–response.
Two extra sessions a week for 6 more weeks removed non-response in everyone; VO₂max gains tracked gains in haemoglobin mass.
The second block had small groups, no control group and added weeks as well as sessions, so time, noise and regression to the mean can't be ruled out.
For an athlete: check the noise, look at several measures, then raise the dose or change the stimulus before deciding you don't respond.

variants.stem: A year-long study with repeated VO₂max tests and a control group finds clear individual differences in response, but different methods label only 11 of 20 people the same way. Which conclusion fits best?

options.text: People truly differ in response, but labelling a person is unreliable
options.why: Right: real variability at the group level and shaky individual labels can both be true.

options.text: Individual differences in response are all noise
options.why: Repeated testing showed differences of relevant size, beyond noise.

options.text: About half of people are true non-responders
options.why: Labels didn't even agree between methods, so no share of non-responders can be read from it.

options.text: The training itself didn't work for the group
options.why: VO₂max rose clearly in the training group compared with control.

variants.stem: A runner wants to know whether a 12-week block really raised his VO₂max. Which plan gives the clearest answer?

options.text: Test several times during and after the block, and look at the trend
options.why: Right: repeated testing spreads the noise over many points, as in the year-long study.

options.text: One maximal test before and one after, done very carefully
options.why: Care helps, but one test at each end still carries the full noise of a difference.

options.text: Compare his gain with the average gain in a published study
options.why: Other people's average says nothing about whether his own change is real.

options.text: Take a genetic test for VO₂max trainability
options.why: No gene test predicts one person's trainability.

variants.stem: A study classes any change in ramp-test peak power within ±3.96% as non-response. A cyclist goes from 300 to 310 W. How is he classed?

options.text: Non-responder: +3.3% is inside ±3.96%
options.why: Right: 10 ÷ 300 = 3.3%, inside the noise band.

options.text: Responder: +10 W is more than 3.96
options.why: This compares watts with a percentage; the threshold is 3.96% of 300 W, about 11.9 W.

options.text: Responder: any rise in power counts
options.why: The threshold exists because small rises can be noise.

options.text: Non-responder: he needed at least +10%
options.why: The cut-off was ±3.96%, the test's typical error, not 10%.

variants.solution: Change = 310 − 300 = 10 W; 10 ÷ 300 × 100 = 3.3%. That is inside ±3.96%, so he is classed a non-responder (3.96% of 300 W ≈ 11.9 W).

variants.stem: Same rule (±3.96% counts as non-response). A triathlete's peak power goes from 250 to 262 W. How is she classed?

options.text: Responder: +4.8% is beyond 3.96%
Non-responder: +12 W is too small to matter
options.why: Judge the change against the noise band in percent: 3.96% of 250 W is only 9.9 W.

options.text: Non-responder: +4.8% is within 2 × 3.96%
options.why: The study's cut-off was 1 × the typical error, not 2 ×.

options.text: Non-responder: +0.048% is inside ±3.96%
options.why: This forgets to multiply by 100: 12 ÷ 250 = 0.048, which is 4.8%.

variants.solution: Change = 262 − 250 = 12 W; 12 ÷ 250 × 100 = 4.8%, beyond 3.96% (9.9 W), so she is a responder.

variants.stem: Same rule (±3.96% counts as non-response). A cyclist's peak power goes from 320 to 332 W. How is he classed?

options.text: Non-responder: +3.75% is inside ±3.96%
options.why: Right: 12 ÷ 320 = 3.75%, just inside the band.

options.text: Responder: +12 W is more than 3.96
options.why: This compares watts with a percentage; 3.96% of 320 W is about 12.7 W.

options.text: Responder: +3.75% rounds up to 4%
options.why: Rounding before comparing changes the answer; 3.75% is below 3.96%.

options.text: Non-responder: power must rise by 3.96% each week
options.why: The threshold applies to the whole block's change.

variants.solution: Change = 332 − 320 = 12 W; 12 ÷ 320 × 100 = 3.75%, inside ±3.96% (12.7 W), so he is classed a non-responder.

variants.stem: In Montero and Lundby's study, how did the share of non-responders change from one to five 60-minute sessions a week?

options.text: It fell steadily, to zero at four and five sessions
It stayed about 20% in every group
options.why: The 'one in five' figure comes from public health studies, not from this dose study.

options.text: It was lowest at three sessions and rose with more
options.why: It kept falling, with no rise at higher doses.

options.text: It fell only between four and five sessions
options.why: Most of the fall came between one and four sessions.

variants.stem: After the extra training in Montero and Lundby's study, what best explained the gains in VO₂max?

options.text: A rise in total haemoglobin mass
options.why: Right: haemoglobin mass was the strongest independent determinant of VO₂max.

options.text: Weight loss
options.why: The study pointed to blood oxygen-carrying capacity, not body mass.

options.text: A higher maximal heart rate
options.why: Maximal heart rate barely changes with training.

options.text: Better pacing in the ramp test
options.why: Power gains followed VO₂max gains, which followed haemoglobin mass.

variants.stem: In a crossover study, a runner gained little VO₂max from 3 weeks of steady running but a lot from 3 weeks of sprint intervals. What does the study suggest about this?

options.text: Response to one type of training doesn't predict response to another
options.why: Right: individual changes after the two programmes weren't positively related.

options.text: He is a non-responder whose interval gain must be noise
options.why: The study found that people often responded to one stimulus but not the other.

options.text: Sprint intervals are better for everyone
options.why: Some people gained more from the steady training; the pattern differed between people.

options.text: His genes block gains from steady running
options.why: Three weeks of one programme can't show a genetic block.

variants.stem: Montero and Lundby retrained only the people whose first 6-week change was smallest, adding two sessions a week for 6 more weeks, with no control group. What weakens the conclusion that higher dose 'abolishes' non-response?

options.text: Regression to the mean and the extra time could raise their scores anyway
options.why: Right: with no control group, people picked for low first scores may score higher next time anyway, and the second block also added weeks, so time and dose are mixed.

options.text: Six weeks is too short a block for VO₂max to change
options.why: VO₂max can rise within 3 weeks; block length isn't the main problem here.

options.text: Peak power in a ramp test can't be measured reliably
options.why: Its typical error was known (3.96%) and used as the threshold.

options.text: The five groups trained at different intensities
options.why: The groups followed the same programme, differing only in sessions per week.

variants.stem: A cyclist trains 3 × 1 h a week for 8 weeks. Her ramp-test peak power is flat on one test before and one after. She concludes she is a non-responder. Best advice?

options.text: Retest, check other measures, then add sessions or change the stimulus
options.why: Right: one pair of tests is noisy, other measures may have moved, and more dose or a new stimulus usually brings a response.

options.text: Accept it: non-response is genetic and fixed
options.why: A dose study removed non-response in everyone with more training; one flat result isn't a verdict.

options.text: Take a genetic test to confirm it
options.why: No gene test predicts trainability.

options.text: Cut training to recover, since flat results mean overtraining
options.why: Three hours a week is a modest dose; too little is more likely than too much.
